transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Name]. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hi, Doctor. Um… I guess I’m here because I’ve maybe taken on a bit too much lately. I’m an artist, and I’ve been saying yes to a lot—projects, workshops, fixing up the studio, client calls—and I was sort of telling myself it was all good momentum. But now the deadlines are piling up, and with the mortgage too, it’s starting to feel like it’s closing in on me. I thought it might be wise to talk to someone before I make a bigger mess of it, if that makes sense.
Do you find yourself feeling anxious or worried most days, even when there isn’t a specific deadline or problem you’re dealing with?

I don’t think so… not most days, no. It’s more when there’s something concrete piling up, like work or bills. I mean, I can be a worrier like anyone, but I wouldn’t want to overstate it. Is that the kind of thing you mean?
Do you find yourself feeling worried or anxious about a number of different things, not just work or bills, and does this worry feel difficult to control?

I’m not sure I’d say it’s a number of different things, no. It’s mostly the practical stuff when it stacks up. I can get tense and go over it in my head, but if there’s not some actual problem in front of me, I don’t think I’m just worrying all the time. I hope that’s a clear enough answer.
When you’re dealing with these practical problems and feel tension, do you notice any physical symptoms like restlessness, muscle tension, trouble sleeping, or feeling fatigued as a result?

A little, yes… though I don’t want to make it sound dramatic. It’s more like I get this kind of humming current in me from the morning, and then sitting still feels almost impossible. So I end up rearranging the studio, drafting proposals, emailing people, fiddling with supplies—just keeping busy because being quiet feels… uncomfortable, I guess. Is that the sort of physical thing you mean?
Do you ever find yourself worrying intensely about situations that, in hindsight, didn’t turn out to be as serious as you initially feared?

I don’t think so… not intensely, anyway. I mean, I’ve probably made things bigger in my head once or twice, like anyone does, but I can’t think of a clear pattern where I’m constantly fearing the worst and then realizing it was nothing. It’s usually tied to something real that needs dealing with. Does that answer it okay?
Do you find that your worrying tends to spiral or feel excessive, even when you know logically that things might not be as bad as they seem?

I don’t think it really spirals, no… at least not in the way you’re describing. If something is unresolved, I may keep turning it over because I want to handle it properly, but I usually feel like there’s a reason for it. I’m not sitting there thinking, “This is irrational and I can’t stop,” if that makes sense. Is that helpful?
Has this feeling of tension or the need to keep busy ever interfered with your ability to focus on your art, interact with others, or affected your sleep or health in a meaningful way?

Yes… I mean, a bit. I’d like to say I’m still managing, and mostly I am, but it has started to spill over.

Some illustration deadlines have slipped, which is embarrassing because I’m usually very careful about that. A couple of colleagues have checked in on me—not in a dramatic way, just sort of noticing I’m stretched thin. And… this is harder to say, but the mortgage is a concern now because I overcommitted to things and spent money I really should have kept aside to keep the studio secure.

I don’t know if that’s what you mean by meaningful, but it’s not nothing, I suppose.
Would you say these feelings of tension and being overwhelmed only really started after these recent pressures with work and money came up, or have they been there even when things were calmer?

I think it’s mostly been since the work and money side of things got complicated… so, about three months now, I suppose. It really seemed to start after I took on the mortgage for the cottage-studio.

Before that, when things were calmer, I don’t remember feeling this overwhelmed in the same way. Not to this degree, anyway. Does that make sense?
Do you find that your anxiety or tension lingers even after a specific problem, like a deadline or financial issue, has been resolved?

I’m not sure I’ve noticed it lingering in that way. Usually if the specific thing is sorted, I do feel some relief… maybe I stay a bit keyed up for a little while, but I wouldn’t want to overstate it.

I suppose I haven’t been paying close attention to whether it carries on after the problem is actually resolved. Is that the kind of thing you mean?
When there are no immediate deadlines, financial issues, or other stressors actively piling up, do you still find yourself feeling anxious or tense, even if there’s nothing specific to worry about?

I think… not usually? Or at least I haven’t really noticed it when there isn’t something concrete going on.

If the day is quiet and there’s no email waiting or bill to think about, I can settle a bit more. I may still feel a little on edge out of habit, but I wouldn’t want to make it sound like I’m anxious for no reason all the time. It seems tied to things actually pressing on me, if that’s a fair way to put it.
Can you recall any periods in the last few months when you felt noticeably anxious or tense for no clear reason, even when there wasn’t anything pressing happening in your life?

Not really that I can clearly point to, no. I mean, I might have had the odd uneasy morning or felt a bit tense, but when I think about it there’s usually been something in the background — money, work, some email I haven’t dealt with.

I don’t want to say “never,” because maybe I haven’t noticed properly, but I can’t recall a definite period where I was anxious for no reason when everything was actually calm. Is that the distinction you’re trying to make?
Would you say that, even when things aren’t extremely busy, you still tend to worry more than most people about everyday matters?

I’m not sure I’d say more than most people, honestly. I do worry about normal things—emails, money, whether I’ve handled something properly—but it feels like the sort of worrying anyone would have.

Maybe I’m not the best judge of what “most people” is, though. I don’t think it’s excessive when things aren’t very busy, but… if you think there’s a better way to gauge that, I’m happy to try.

Would you say that your anxiety or worry tends to show up even in everyday situations that most people wouldn't think much about, or does it only come up when there's a clear and significant stressor involved?

I think it’s more the second one — when there’s a clear stressor. At least that’s how it seems to me.

I don’t usually get worked up over, say, a normal errand or an ordinary conversation unless there’s something bigger attached to it, like money or something I’ve put off. I mean, I may fuss a little, but I wouldn’t want to exaggerate it. It doesn’t feel like I’m anxious about every little everyday thing for no reason. Does that answer it the way you mean?
Do you find it hard to control your worrying, even when you try to focus on something else or remind yourself that things might work out?

I don’t think so, not in a way that feels really out of control. If I’m worried about something specific, it can sit in the back of my mind, and I might circle around it a bit, but usually I can distract myself or tell myself to just deal with it when I can.

I mean, maybe I’m making it sound tidier than it is, but I wouldn’t say I’m constantly fighting with my thoughts or unable to focus. Does that make sense?
Even in moments when there’s no real pressure or stressor, do you ever notice a low-level anxiety or worry that’s just kind of present, even if it’s not about anything specific?

I don’t think so… not really. I mean, I have ordinary background thoughts like anyone does, but I wouldn’t say there’s this anxiety just sitting there for no reason.

If there’s something actually going on, then yes, I can worry. But when things are calm, I’m usually okay. At least, that’s how I understand it. Is that the kind of distinction you’re asking about?
Would you say that your worrying about everyday matters feels difficult to control, even when you try to shift your attention or reason with yourself?

I still wouldn’t say it feels difficult to control, no. If it’s everyday stuff, I can usually redirect myself or sort of talk myself down.

I might come back to it later if it’s unfinished, but it doesn’t feel like it takes over or that I can’t reason with myself. I hope I’m not repeating myself too much — that’s just honestly how it seems to me.
Would you say that, overall, you’ve felt anxious or worried on more days than not over the past several months, even when things weren’t especially stressful?

No, I don’t think so. Not more days than not, especially if there wasn’t anything really stressful going on.

I mean, I have normal worries, of course, and I don’t want to make it sound like I’m perfectly calm all the time. But overall, over the past several months, I wouldn’t describe myself as anxious most days. Is that the kind of answer you mean?
Looking back over the past few months, would you say that you’ve felt excessive anxiety or worry about things more days than not, even if it wasn’t overwhelming?

I don’t think I’d call it excessive, no. I’ve had things on my mind here and there, like anyone would, but not most days in that ongoing way.

I’m trying to answer it accurately and not just say what sounds better… but looking back, I really don’t think anxiety or worry has been a more-days-than-not kind of thing for me.

inference_history.note: Initial presentation suggests possible stress-related disorders, depressive disorders, and anxiety disorders as leading differentials based on reported pressure, overwhelm, and concerns about managing responsibilities.

The patient’s symptoms appear to be primarily stress-related, tied to identifiable external pressures (e.g., work, bills), rather than pervasive anxiety or depressive disorders. This makes adjustment disorder (F43.2) the most likely category. The presence of anxiety symptoms in response to stressors supports F43.22, though other subtypes remain under consideration based on evolving symptom emphasis. Major depressive disorder (F32, F33), generalized anxiety disorder (F41.1), and other primary anxiety disorders are less likely given the absence of persistent, unprovoked anxiety or core depressive features. PTSD (F43.1), somatic symptom (F45), and other neurotic or personality-related disorders (F44, F60) are also less likely based on the current narrative, though not fully ruled out.

The patient's anxiety appears to be primarily situational and tied to real-life stressors rather than being excessive or uncontrollable. This makes generalized anxiety disorder (F43.20, F43.21, F43.22) less likely. The presence of mild physical symptoms and difficulty relaxing points toward an adjustment disorder with anxiety (F43.8) or unspecified anxiety (F43.9).

The patient's anxiety appears to be primarily situational and tied to concrete stressors, without clear evidence of excessive or uncontrollable worry, physical symptoms of anxiety, or significant impairment in daily functioning. This supports consideration of mild anxiety, but no definitive diagnosis can be made at this time.

However, the anxiety is not pervasive, is not present in the absence of stressors, and does not meet full criteria for generalized anxiety disorder (F41.1) or adjustment disorder with anxiety (F43.2.2). F43.8 (Other reactions to stress) is most appropriate given the subthreshold but clinically significant anxiety tied to identifiable stressors without a more specific pattern. F43.9 (Reaction, unspecified) remains a differential due to the borderline nature of symptom frequency and control.
